utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you call the case, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Mr. Brdjanin, can you hear me in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. I hear and I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. You may sit down. Appearances for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Ann Sutherland for the Prosecution assisted by Denise Gustin, case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you and good afternoon to you. Appearances for Radoslav Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. I'm John Ackerman with Milan Trbojevic and Marela Jevtovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Any preliminaries? No? Yes?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Ms. Korner is unfortunately unable to be here to address Your Honours in relation to the sitting days. We have been advised that the plenary may not now be heard on the 2nd and 3rd of December and may still be held on the 11th, 12th and 13th of December.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It will be held apparently on the 12th. That won't change our decision to sit on the 11th, 12th and 13th so we will be sitting on those days.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And also on the 4th of December? I'm sorry, our schedule will not change?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. What I may suggest to you but it depends on a reply I'm expecting from my secretary is if you can also sit or get a witness or do something on the 3rd, that's Tuesday, then probably we would be able to do that but I'm -- I was hoping to have an answer before the sitting. Unfortunately, I don't. We won't be sitting Thursday and Friday of next week and Monday, the following Monday, the 2nd, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: That's the 28th and 29th of November and the 2nd of December.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm very happy to say that we will still sit on the 11th, 12th and 13th of December.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Definitely.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Because I was instructed to register the strongest protest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Definitely, we can't stay playing around with dates like that. We took a decision yesterday and I will not budge from it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, we may not be able to get a witness for the 3rd of December because all these witnesses have been contacted and the dates have been changed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That suits me fine actually because I have one of the other cases that needs -- has three motions that need to be decided in it and I think that's the only day I have on which I can really dedicate some extra hours but if it is necessary to sit on the 3rd, we will sit on the 3rd.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It has been decided now that it will be on the 12th.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And the Prosecution will let the Chamber know as soon as possible and Mr. Ackerman if we are able to have a witness here for the 3rd of December but given the recent change I don't think that's going to be a possibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just inform me and later on during the sitting, I should know precisely where I stand on the 3rd because much depends on others. So the next witness, I think, if I remember well, enjoys some -- yes, Mr. Ackerman, I'm sorry. I didn't recognise you before.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Judge, I have two rather brief matters. I filed today and there was a courtesy copy I think given to you of my first response to the Rule 92 bis motion where I discuss four of the witnesses and I'll continue to work and file the rest as soon as I possibly can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Also, just in the interests of making the record as accurate as possible, when I suggested to the witness yesterday that there was a unit with a 90 per cent attrition rate, I was incorrect about that. I went and checked the transcript. The testimony is at page 11068. There was a regiment of 1.000 soldiers, 928 deserted from that regiment so the actual desertion rate was 92.8 per cent rather than 90 per cent. And that's all I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. The witness --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Before we proceed with the witness may I tender into evidence the photographs and maps from Witness 7.204?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please. Please do.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Therefore, Exhibit P1517-1 to 19 -- sorry, 1 to 21, is P1517/S210. And where the photographs that were also marked is 210/S will then become P1517/210/S or whatever the photograph number was. I think it will be clear when the photographs have been marked. Exhibit number P1518 will be what was S211 and S211/S so that will be P1518/2 -- S211, P1518/S is -- /S 211/S. It's very confusing. P1519 -- Your Honour this was in relation to the agreement I thought we had in court yesterday as to how the exhibits would be numbered. They would have our number, then slash, the Stakic number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know what's going on I'm totally confused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're not the only one but I would suggest that you interrupt Ms. Sutherland, the least possible, because if she gets confused too then we are in a big mess.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I actually received the numbering from the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The important thing is this.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: To have it on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: To have it on the record, exactly and if the Registrar is following the chronological and logical order of your presentation, then I am happy, I don't need to know more. I know that you may not be as happy as I am but you can check afterwards, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, the important thing is that when one looks at yesterday's transcript, one should be able by the designation that were made in the record yesterday to be able to find what it is we are talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think if I can read Ms. Sutherland well that's what she's doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If we are changing numbers today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think we are changing from what I could follow.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, it relates to the witness who testified the day before yesterday, Witness 7.204, BT32. I explained as I took him through his evidence in chief that we would not be going through every single photograph and every single map but they were going to be tendered to the courtroom as an exhibit and I'm simply giving those maps and photographs an exhibit number and as agreed yesterday it would be our exhibit number/the Stakic exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So I've just done the photographs and the two maps. So P1519 will be P1519/S212. P1520 will be P1520/S213. And P1521 has already been tendered, I'm sorry, I'm reading down the exhibit list I was just given but that's already been tendered that was in relation to witness Poljak. And we will provide Mr. Ackerman with a list of the exhibits as we have done with the Registrar so that he knows exactly what exhibit is what and the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That would be most useful. So now, the next witness enjoys a pseudonym plus facial distortion?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I mentioned voice distortion when I raised the matter last time but he only has pseudonym and image distortion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And image distortion. Shall now -- he will, however, come into the courtroom and I want to make sure that he does not show up in -- yes, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You mentioned three things yesterday that you wanted me to respond to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, 92, 94, and protective measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. That's what I thought. On protective measures, Your Honour, what I would really like to do is just make it clear in the record that with regard to any motion for protective measures, I do not oppose any protective measure short of closed session and in every case I oppose closed sessions and that way I won't have to file a bunch of paper every time they do something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I think you were late in any case. But Ms. Sutherland, please refer that to Ms. Korner and my staff knows precisely how to go about the protective measures motion. 12th protective measures motion. Yes, please. So we can remain in open session, Madam Chuqing, as I understand it and now as soon as the gentleman takes his seat --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon. Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So this is the second time you have come to this Tribunal to give evidence so you ought to be familiar with the procedure. The usher will be handing you the text of a solemn declaration to speak the truth and the whole truth and nothing but the truth in the course of your testimony so please make that solemn declaration now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Witness answered through interpreter].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. You may sit down. I'll be very brief in my introduction to you. You would have noticed that I did not refer to you by your name, and that behind you there is a sort of a curtain plus other panels that conceal you from the public. The reason is something that you are certainly aware of. You have asked for certain protective measures to be put in place and we have agreed on two basic protective measures. One is that you will be given a pseudonym, a number, and that's how you will be known in this trial, and referred to. And secondly, that although this remains an open session, a public session, your image is distorted so anyone who looks at the monitor will see what you probably are seeing now on your screen, if you are on monitor video mode. Having said that, you will be asked a series of questions by Ms. Sutherland, who is appearing for the Prosecution. You will not -- first, you will not be asked the amount of questions you were asked in Stakic. The reason is very simple. We have a transcript of your testimony in Stakic and that is going to be considered in this case too. So there is no need to repeat certain questions, but there will be some questions which Ms. Sutherland will put to you to add upon what you have already testified in Stakic and to clarify other matters to us in this trial. At the end of the set of questions put to you by the Prosecution and we call that examination-in-chief, you will be cross-examined by Mr. Ackerman for the accused, who is Mr. Radoslav Brdjanin in this particular case. Ms. Sutherland, he is all yours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, you testified --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think he needs to identify himself first.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Gustin.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can you look at this piece of paper and it can be first showed to the Defence and can you confirm without saying your name that that is in fact your name written on that piece of paper?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Usher could you please show it to Mr. Ackerman and then to us?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could that be under seal as Prosecution Exhibit P1528?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, you testified in the Stakic trial on the 10th and 11th of June, 2002 and you have reviewed your testimony by listening to the audiotapes. As His Honour has just explained to you, your Stakic testimony is now going to be admitted into this trial pursuant to Rule 92 bis along with any exhibits that were tendered through you in that trial. Except for two portions of your testimony which have been redacted from the transcript, which we will deal with later on today. I will briefly summarise some of the matters that you testified about in the Stakic trial over the two days. I will also be asking you some clarifying questions and some questions in addition to your Stakic testimony.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I tender the bundle as Exhibit P1529?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, it is being so admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: May we move into private session so that I can ask some background questions of the witness on a topic which specifically requires private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Registrar, please, let's go into private session for a while.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, we are now in open session so bear that in mind when giving your answers so as not to reveal the identity -- your identity.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to play a tape now. It was provided to the booth in Courtroom III yesterday and I hope we have it -- yes, we have.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, I would like you to watch this videotape and tell the Court if there is anyone on that videotape that you recognise and we can have the videotape paused. The quality is very, very bad and I hope that when the videotape is paused, you will still be able to recognise who you wish to point out to the Court. The videotape I want to play is Prosecution Exhibit P1129 and it's V000-0084 for the AV's benefit. And it needs to be started at point 11.36.26.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could you stop? Could the video be fast-forwarded to 11.36.26, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You need to tell us when you want us to pause.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could the sound be cut, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I start?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes. Could the video be rewound, please, to the start of the meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can see here Mr. Stakic, Mr. Simo Drljaca, Mr. Kovacevic -- Dr. Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The video is paused at 11.36.24.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Who is the doctor first of all with -- Dr. Stakic, whereabouts is he sitting in that frame?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27
utterances.text: Straight, in the -- in the middle of the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So he's sitting at the end of the table to the left? As you look --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Drljaca, where is he sitting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27
utterances.text: On his left, or rather, yes, yes, on his left, as I am looking at the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So, on Stakic's right but to the -- as you look at the photograph, to the left of Dr. Stakic, what colour shirt does he have on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27
utterances.text: That's right. Drljaca has a white T-shirt or shirt, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And Dr. Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27
utterances.text: Dr. Kovacevic is in the very corner and he's not shown in his entirety. He's next to Simo Drljaca. Maybe there is somebody else there but here on the screen, he's in the left corner of the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Is he clean shaven or does he have a mustache?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27
utterances.text: He has a mustache.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could the video be played again?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could you stop?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you recognise anyone in that frame and we have freezed it at 11.36.34.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27
utterances.text: I think, although I'm not a hundred per cent sure because I've only seen Zeljaja three times in my life but I think that this could be Radmilo Zeljaja, but I'm not positive entirely.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Whereabouts is he sitting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27
utterances.text: But I think it could be him. Here at the very beginning, on the right-hand side of the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: In the military uniform?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27
utterances.text: In a military uniform, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could the video please be played?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Simo Drljaca, Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Stop the video, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know the others.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Stop the video completely, thank you. Could the witness please be shown Prosecution Exhibit P1127? That is the map of the Prijedor area. Usher, could you bring me the exhibit and I will fold it in such a way that it can be placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, I would like you to point out for the Court, please, the following places, using the pointer. First of all, to the Prijedor town itself. If you could point out using the ELMO machine on your left, if you could place the pointer on the machine on your left, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27
utterances.text: Here.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could you point now to Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27
utterances.text: This is Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... The village of Kozarusa?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27
utterances.text: This is Kozarusa.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The village of Kamicani?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27
utterances.text: This is where the village of Kamicani is.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Benkovac or Mrakovica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27
utterances.text: This is Mrakovica here and right here we have Benkovac.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And two places that we will be discussing in just one moment, the hamlet or village of Dera?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could you point --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27
utterances.text: There is a place called Dera.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could you point on the map to approximately where that is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27
utterances.text: That place is here, just in front of the village Rajkovici between Kozarac, as you travel from Kozarac to Mrakovica, approximately here.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And I think in your prior testimony you said it was approximately two kilometres from Kozarac town?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could you also please point to where the Orlovci checkpoint was? Orlovci checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27
utterances.text: Orlovci. This is Kozarusa, Mujkanovici. Right here, right here between the place called Kalate. This is where there was a checkpoint on the asphalt road which goes from Prijedor to Banja Luka, somewhere here.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You're pointing at the moment to the road marked in red between Prijedor and Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you. I've finished with the map. You testified in the Stakic trial that after the takeover on the 30th of April, 1992, a mixed checkpoint was set up in Kozarac at the junctions of the Prijedor-Banja Luka road and the Kozarac-Trnopolje road and there was done for security reasons.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is at page 4264.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And you also testified that there was a Serb checkpoint at Orlovci which you've just pointed to on the map. You testified that on the 24th of May, 1992, about conversations Zeljaja had with Osman Didovic in relation to a military convoy passing Kozarac. This is at page 4273. And you discussed a subsequent telephone call a short time later, perhaps some 20 minutes later, from Zeljaja to say that the convoy had been attacked at Jakupovici, and you said that Didovic was then going to see what happened when the shelling of Kozarac began. You testified that as you recall, Zeljaja, that as you recall, Zeljaja had said that the convoy was moving from Prijedor to Banja Luka. You also testified that given the short time between the two telephone conversations, i.e. the first conversation with Zeljaja about the convoy passing and the subsequent telephone conversation some 20 minutes later to say that it had been attacked at Jakupovici, you testified that the convoy would not have had enough time to start its journey from Prijedor and reach Jakupovici where it was allegedly attacked, and you said this at page 4384 of the transcript. Therefore, it was your belief that the convoy was in fact travelling from Banja Luka towards Prijedor. My question today is regardless of the direction in which the convoy was travelling, given that you testified that the shelling started shortly after Zeljaja called Didovic to inform him about the alleged attack, would this mean that tanks would have already had to have been in place for that to happen, for the shelling to have occurred immediately?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27
utterances.text: Yes. On that 24th of May, the plan which was described to us by Zeljaja was begun because Zeljaja told us that he had already had coordinates. It was impossible to put or position heavy artillery on the elevations around Kozarac within 20 minutes. From the first conversation with Major Zeljaja with the commander of the police, only 20 minutes passed before the first shell landed on Kozarac. And after that, from many directions, they started shelling Kozarac. Very intensely. So that the convoy that had been announced by Major Zeljaja was probably just an excuse for starting shelling Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: In your Stakic testimony, you described in detail the attack on Kozarac on the 24th of May, 1992. This is at page 4273 and following. That the attack began around 1300 hours and the intense shelling continued until the following day. You testified that the police commander Didovic had moved the police base to a house in Dera and you've just pointed that out for Their Honours on the map, where an improvised hospital was set up and that you were at that house during the shelling of Kozarac. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: In your testimony you mentioned Azra Blazevic and Dr. Jusuf Pasic being there. Do you know a Dr. Idriz Merdzanic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Was he also there at the house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You testified that on the 25th of May, 1992, Didovic established a radio connection with Zeljaja and that Zeljaja stated that the inhabitants of Kozarac and the surrounding areas had to form a column with the policemen leading the column with white flags and to gather at the Limenka bus stop. You described how you and many of the inhabitants gathered there at the bus stop on the 26th of May, 1992. You stated you saw a number of soldiers in different uniforms, olive grey, blue camouflage and black uniforms with insignia on caps. You mentioned that you saw a number of houses or houses burning in the neighbouring villages of Brdjani and Kozarusa. You stated that 20 or so Autotransport buses were at Limenka when the column arrived and you were ordered on to one of the buses with the other policemen and were you taken to the police station in Prijedor, the SUP. You testified that from the SUP, you were taken with a number of other men to the Keraterm camp and when you arrived there, there were approximately 50 men there, including the elected president of the Prijedor municipality, Muhamed Cehajic, who you noticed had been beaten.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown Prosecution Exhibits P1128.14 and P1128.15? The photographs?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, looking at P1128.14, what is shown in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27
utterances.text: This photograph depicts the Keraterm camp near Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can you point to where you were detained?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27
utterances.text: On that day, we were brought into this garage here, this first one here.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And you're pointing to the end room to the left of the photograph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't hear, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: At ground floor level.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And P1128.15. Again, is that another photo of Keraterm from a different angle?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you. In your testimony, you described -- I'm finished with the photographs. In your testimony you described how you spent the night of the 26th of May and the 27th of May detained in the camp. Were you ever told why you were being detained at Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You testified that in the afternoon of the 27th of May, you were ordered by guards on to the Autotransport Prijedor buses, and this is at page 4286, and that those buses left the camp at around 4.00 or 5.00 p.m. And arrived at the Omarska camp in the early hours of the following morning, the distance being approximately 28 to 30 kilometres away. You described how when you arrived at the Omarska camp you heard sounds of shooting and of glass breaking. You mentioned the name of three people, the names of three people who were taken off the bus whether you first arrived at Omarska who you've never seen again and that's at pages 4303 to 4304. You were detained at the Omarska camp from the early hours of the 28th of May until the 6th of August, 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I know we have the whole day but what seems to be going on is you're just being told what the transcript says that you've been provided with. Rarely is the witness asked a question and I thought the whole purpose of providing you the transcripts was so that we wouldn't have to do this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Indeed you are right. On the other hand, what I notice Ms. Sutherland is doing is she's preparing the way for a question every so often. And to do that, apparently she needs to remind the witness of when he stated. If you can condense it and go straight to the question, that will be much better because it would reduce the testimony substantially but it's up to you. I mean I wouldn't like to interfere much. But perhaps I think in a way, Mr. Ackerman may be right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Could the witness be shown photograph P1128.18?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, what is shown in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27
utterances.text: This photograph depicts the Omarska camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could you point on the machine on your left to where you were detained?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27
utterances.text: It can't be seen very well from here, because I was in a room number 15, which is located on this side, upstairs. In front of this building, there was the entrance door which I passed through on the 28th.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown P1128.4?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Would you point on that photograph to where you were detained?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27
utterances.text: This photograph depicts the -- among other things, the door through which I went through, and then on the right-hand side, upstairs here, there is the room number 15, which consisted of two rooms.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The room you're pointing to what was that commonly referred to, that building, that long building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27
utterances.text: Hangar.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your room -- you pointed to the entrance or exit door and your room was to the right of the door?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27
utterances.text: Yes, upstairs on the right-hand side, the first door on your right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could you please point to the administration building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27
utterances.text: The administration building was here next to the restaurant where we went for our meals, right here.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And the other two buildings shown on the model?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27
utterances.text: This one here, a small house that you can see here, is something that we called the "white house." The last time I said, and I can confirm it now, that the real name for that house would be the black house.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And you gave the reasons why in your transcript so we won't go into that. The other building on the photograph, the building on the right-hand corner, what building -- what name was that referred to by?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27
utterances.text: We called this building the red house.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you. I've finished with the photograph. You were detained in room 15 for the whole of your detention except for one day that you spent on the pista. Were you ever told why you were being detained in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27
utterances.text: No. Nobody ever addressed us and explained to us the reasons for our detention there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You testified that detainee -- that the maltreatment of detainees was constant and you described in detail about a beating that you suffered, which we will not go into but Their Honours can read at pages 4295 and following, and the injuries that you suffer today from that beating, and they are on page 4301. I want to clarify something that you were asked in cross-examination in the Stakic trial. You were questioned and asked about whether you were aware, since the establishment -- since the since you were there since the establishment of the Omarska camp, whether you were familiar with the fact that during the first ten days of June, quite a few people, approximately 70 per day, were released from the camp, having previously been interrogated. You stated that you were aware of this. Did you ever see any of these people who were released in the camp again?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27
utterances.text: Yes. It is true that during the first ten days, maybe less, some people who had been interviewed were released. However, I saw again Fadil Basic in room 15, although he had been interrogated previously and released, and then returned again. I also saw Ante Slutaj who was the secretary of the school in Kozarac, and also there were other people who again were returned into Omarska camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: During your detention in the Omarska camp, did you see anyone from the Serb authorities in the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27
utterances.text: While I was at the Omarska camp, since I was staying in room number 15, I did not have the opportunity of seeing anyone except a couple of times, Simo Drljaca, but I heard, or we heard, when a delegation came --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think "I heard or we heard".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let him say it and I'll decide afterwards whether to admit it or whether it have it redacted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead. You heard?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, first of all can you tell me -- can you tell the Trial Chamber what you heard and who did you hear it from and in what circumstances?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And when.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This arrival of the delegation to the Omarska camp, I heard about it from Ante Slutaj, the school secretary from Kozarac. The man who that morning, when the delegation arrived, was taken out with another 15 inmates, whom the guard took past the white house to the latrine, and then after they finished, he left them on the pista. They left in the morning hours because the preparations in expectation of the visit began in the morning already, so that he was present when the delegation arrived. We, in room 15, were able to hear the chanting, the fanatical chanting, "This is Serbia," the singing of songs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Who the components of this delegation were. Who composed this delegation? That's what we want to know. We don't want the whole story.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The delegation that Ante Slutaj told me about comprised Brdjanin from Banja Luka, Kupresanin, Simo Miskovic, Simo Drljaca, Major Zeljaja, Arsic, and he also told me that there was a person called Vukic there as well. I don't know him. He told me that he was a school teacher from Banja Luka, and he knew him because he was also a teacher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: When did he tell you this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He told me about it when he came back. I don't know exactly what time that was, but maybe it was about noon, when he returned to room 15, after the arrival of the delegation, together with these other people who had left the room to go to the latrine that morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, you -- what did Ante tell you when he returned to the room? You began earlier by saying that it they were -- you heard that they were singing songs. What other information did Ante tell you besides who was in the delegation, if anything?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If it's something that already results from the transcript, you can go direct straight to. Otherwise, we leave it at that. First of all, did he tell you anything else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ante Slutaj said that they had to raise three fingers and chant, "This is Serbia," that they had to sing songs.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Moving on to another topic, you described the horrific conditions in the camp and that was at page 4306, and you testified about seeing bodies in Tam trucks and that around the 24th and 25th of July, two persons who were detained in the same room as you told you that they had loaded around 100 dead bodies from the red house and that the bodies had been mutilated, and this is at page 4308. I want to move now to the 6th of August, 1992. You testified that on that date, a large number of buses arrived and your name was called out, along with many other of the other detainees and then you were placed on these buses and taken to the Manjaca camp. Again, the buses took all night until the early hours of the morning to reach the Manjaca camp and you testified that upon your arrival two men were called from the buses who you have never seen again.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown photographs -- the following photographs which haven't been given an exhibit number yet? And, Your Honour, these were not on my proposed list of exhibits although I did list that I would use the main bundle, P1128, of which they come from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What's the ERN number?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm trying to find it, Your Honour. 00396712 will become -- if we can mark that as P1128.31? And then 00464997, which will be marked Prosecution Exhibit P1128.32? And the last one, ERN 00456983 which will become Prosecution Exhibit P1128.33.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Looking first at P1128.31, what is shown in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27
utterances.text: This photograph shows the entrance to the Manjaca camp. This is the gate through which we entered the Manjaca camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The stable where you were detained, is that shown on that photograph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27
utterances.text: You don't see this building, the stable, on this photograph, but it's third in line. It's next to the kitchen, where we had lunch. It's the third building in order, that you can see on this photograph.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Looking now at Prosecution Exhibit P1128.32, do you -- can it be placed that way? Thank you. Up -- what is shown in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27
utterances.text: You can see the inside of those stables where we stayed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you recognise anyone in that photograph? And if so, can you just, using the pointer, place the pointer on the machine?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27
utterances.text: This is Muharem Besic, called Cicak. This is Samir Kusuran from Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Muhamed Besic, where is he from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27
utterances.text: From Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And he's the man in the orangey-coloured jumper in the foreground of the photograph? And the man you referred to as Kusuran --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: -- is to his left as we look at the photograph in the dark-coloured jumper?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27
utterances.text: This man, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Looking at Prosecution Exhibit P1128.33, what is shown in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27
utterances.text: This photograph also shows the interior of the stables where we were placed while in Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And you can see the rails on either side of the photograph behind the detainees seated on the floor. What's behind those rails on either side?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27
utterances.text: Inmates were also behind those rails. The metal rails were used to tie up cattle, cows and cattle to the rails.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Before the detainees were placed there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You would -- thank you, I've finished with the photograph. Sir, you were detained in Manjaca camp from the 6th of August until the 18th of December, 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Were you ever told -- were you ever told why you were being detained in Manjaca camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27
utterances.text: We were told once when Mr. Brdjanin came, and addressed us, that -- and that was the only time that anybody addressed us inmates from the camp and told us why we were there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately when this visit to the camp was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27
utterances.text: I don't know the exact date, because our watches were taken away from us already at Omarska and nobody returned them so I didn't know what time it was or what day it was, but this happened before the camp was disbanded, the camp at Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court what Mr. Brdjanin told you at the Manjaca camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27
utterances.text: On that occasion, Mr. Brdjanin was accompanied by the camp commander, the deputy camp commander, Spaga. He spoke to us.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What did he say?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27
utterances.text: Spaga told him that we were men who raped Serbian women, and who killed Serbian children. After that, he addressed us and said that captured Serbs do not have such conditions as the ones that we had. He said that he was doing everything to send us to third countries, and after that, which was usual, he blamed the then authorities, the SDA, for everything that was happening to us. The SDA authorities headed by Alija Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: When you say, "He" are you referring to Spaga or Mr. Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27
utterances.text: Mr. Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: How did you know that it was Mr. Brdjanin that addressed you? How did he introduce himself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27
utterances.text: Mr. Brdjanin didn't have any need to introduce himself, because already since the first pre-election party rallies and right until the beginning of the war, he frequently appeared on television, on radio. He was a public figure, a politician, and it wasn't difficult to recognise him.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: When he appeared on the television or on the radio, what did you hear him say? What was the general gist of the contents of what you heard him say?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27
utterances.text: Most times when Mr. Brdjanin spoke, he mentioned generally Turks, balijas, the story that Banja Luka was Serb, and during such speeches, all three national parties said the same things.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So you said that you heard Mr. Brdjanin -- saw Mr. Brdjanin on television and heard him on the radio since the first pre-election party rallies and right up until the beginning of the war. Just so that it's crystal clear can you put a time period on this? When were the first multi-party elections?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27
utterances.text: 1991, 1990. He started to appear at the election rallies.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And when you say?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27
utterances.text: Starting from 1990.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: When you say up until the war, are you referring to what month in 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27
utterances.text: I think right up until the time that I had the opportunity, before I went to the camp, to Omarska, until then I was able to see and hear Mr. Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, if that's an appropriate time to break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you have much longer?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I don't. I wish to play a video which may take a little time, maybe 15 minutes, and a few other questions. So maybe half an hour at the max.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. We'll break now. Can I suggest that we break for 15 minutes only? Is that okay? 15 minutes' break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, it has been reported to me that as soon as we left the courtroom, your client addressed the witness directly, calling him a liar and using other disparaging terms. I don't know if you were still in the courtroom when this happened or not and whether you are aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I know only this, Your Honour, that my client reacted in a way that any of us might react when someone tells a complete untruth about us but I don't think he spoke directly to the witness. I think he was telling us that the witness had lied and that he couldn't understand why the witness would lie the way he did under oath in a court of law, but I think the communication was coming directly from Mr. Brdjanin to his lawyers and I don't think he ever spoke directly to the witness. I think that's not true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Has the incident been filmed? By any chance?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm not addressing you. Can the technicians please confirm to me whether the incident was filmed or not?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, we stop recording as soon as you leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would like to have a written report on this, Madam Registrar, by next Monday. In the meantime, I'm going to ask the witness did Mr. Brdjanin address you directly after we left the courtroom? Did he speak to you or did he just pass comments which you heard?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Brdjanin, upon your leaving the courtroom, pointed his fingers at me and said that I lied, that I'm a liar, that he was never at Manjaca. I wouldn't ask for protection without a good reason, and this is why this really hurt me personally because there were 600 people in the stable which he entered in Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Is very simple, whether he addressed you directly or whether he just passed comments as Mr. Ackerman said to Mr. Ackerman himself.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He didn't come right here but he pointed towards me and said I was a liar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Were you still present in the courtroom, Ms. Sutherland?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, I was, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. And Ms. Gustin?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Ms. Gustin was in the courtroom but was unaware of what occurred.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Madam Chuqing, please, I want a full report as to who was here at the time and who would be in a position to give evidence. Yes, Mr. Trbojevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your permission, Your Honours, since I speak the language of our client, he did indeed point his hand in the direction of the witness, but I was sure that he in fact spoke to us, to the Defence counsel, when he said, "This man is a liar." I think that was the essence of what transpired here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's the first time we left before the witness did and he took advantage of it. We'll deal with it when the time comes, Mr. Trbojevic. Yes, in the meantime you may proceed with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If he thinks that he's past -- that this is past and forgotten, he is very badly mistaken, he doesn't know me. He's very badly mistaken. Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir I want to go back to Manjaca. You said just a moment ago that Brdjanin came into the stable where there was some 600 other odd detainees. Was anyone else with Mr. Brdjanin when he came into the stable?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27
utterances.text: In addition to Mr. Brdjanin, there was camp commander and his deputy, whom we used to call Spaga.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... You did mention Mr. Spaga before. Was there anyone else besides camp personnel with Mr. Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I want to move now before I move to another topic, I want to ask you, go back to two matters that we discussed before the break. The first one was in relation to the question I asked you in clarifying something that you had said in cross-examination in the Stakic case, about the number of prisoners who had been released in the first days of the camp being open. You said that you were in room 15, which was on the upper floor of the hangar building and therefore you were not able to be in a position to see things in the camp. My question is this:

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think this has been asked and dealt with repeatedly and what the Prosecutor is trying to do is get the witness to change his testimony about 70 people a day being released from the camp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How can you say that? We haven't heard the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, she is going back to the same issue that she talked to him about before. She wasn't satisfied with his answer. She's trying again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would still wait for the question first.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I failed to ask a question when I asked the witness last time and that was: How do you know that there were in fact 70 people were day as was put to you in cross-examination. How are you aware that it was 70 people per day?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The witness testified under oath in Stakic, Your Honour, that 70 people a day were released from camp during the month of June.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He's being asked to state now how he's aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think the Prosecution is trying to impeach their witness and that's not proper. They're not permitted to impeach their own witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think that's the case. He's being asked how he came to know this.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution could have asked a question in re-examination in the Stakic case but didn't and is asking the witness now how he came to know that 70 people were released per day. He has already testified that some people were released. I'm just asking him whether he knows about the number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You've heard the question. Please answer it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The last time during the cross-examination, Mr. Lukic asked me a question as follows: Do I know that during the first days of the Omarska camp, on a daily basis, after interrogation, 70 people were released? Therefore, I was unable -- I did not have an opportunity to count the people leaving the camp. All I know is that in the first days, the people who had been interrogated were released and then afterwards some of them were brought back.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I also asked you a question in relation to the -- around the 24th and 25th of July, that two people who were detained in your room told you that around 100 bodies had been taken from the red house. Do you know the origin of these hundred people? If you do, say so. If you don't, then please say that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27
utterances.text: About 100 of these people, they were from Omarska, and prior to that, they were from Prijedor area, from Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I now want to move to another topic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown some photographs which will become part of P1128? The first one has the ERN number 0039-4827. That will become P1128.34.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, what is shown on that photograph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27
utterances.text: This photograph depicts Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could you point, using the pointer, on to the machine on your left, could you point to the mosques in the town of Kozarac and name them, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27
utterances.text: This mosque here is called Mutnik mosque. This one here.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can you just pause. The mosque you're pointing to is to the right-hand side of the photograph near a white two or three storey building; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The next mosque?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27
utterances.text: The mosque in Kalata.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And you're pointing to the mosque on the right-hand side of the photograph with a red roof and the minaret?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And the third one?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27
utterances.text: The mosque in Kozarusa.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And now you're pointing to the middle of the photograph, just before the hills, and there is the white minaret; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown Prosecution Exhibit P1128.25?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, just quickly because we need to move a little bit faster, could you show -- tell me what -- tell the Court what's depicted in that photograph. On the left-hand side is a photograph of what?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27
utterances.text: On the left-hand side, we can see the Mutnik mosque in Kozarac which was photographed in 1984 during the Olympic Games and then this is the cinema building in Kozarac and the elementary school in Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And you pointed at the cinema building being the photograph on the top right-hand corner?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And the elementary school in Kozarac being the bottom left-hand photograph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could the witness now be shown this photograph, ERN number 00393194, which will become P1128.35?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, what is shown in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27
utterances.text: This is the Mutnik mosque which was destroyed in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: That is the same building that is in the photograph -- the exhibit you just saw, P1128.25, the photograph on the left-hand side of that exhibit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, the Mutnik mosque, the destroyed Mutnik mosque is already in evidence as P1128.26. No. I'm now told it's not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No it's not. In fact 11 -- that's the -- another building on which another witness testified.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's a wrong ERN number and the ERN number -- can I have the exhibit, please? Thank you. I'm sorry, the exhibit -- the ERN number which I -- I said was 00393191, not 3194. And so that is now Prosecution Exhibit PP1128.35, which is what was discussed a moment ago. Could the witness please be shown this photograph, ERN number 00393202? Which will become Prosecution Exhibit P1128.36?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, very quickly, what is in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27
utterances.text: This photograph depicts the mosque in Kalata that had been destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could you now be given this photograph ERN number 003933081 which will be P1128.37?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27
utterances.text: This photograph shows the Serbian church in Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you. I have finished with the photographs. Sir, in the Stakic trial, you testified -- you named eight policemen that you knew from the Prijedor municipality who were killed in the Omarska camp and you also named seven or so policemen who had been missing since the conflict and that was at page 4314.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown Prosecution Exhibit P1234? I apologise. This was not on the list of exhibits but was a document that was read out in the Stakic trial as Exhibit P-- S130. It's in his transcript at page 432 -- 4330.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, looking at the -- do you have the document in your own language?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27
utterances.text: In English.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: It must be a double-sided document. Sir, can you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, because it wasn't on the list, I have no way of knowing what --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Neither do we.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: -- what we are talking about. I'm also becoming concerned. The original estimate was 30 minute direct, then it was an hour and an a half.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It was three-quarters of an hour to an hour and a half.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I don't know if I'm able to complete a cross-examination today and that really interferes with what's happening on Monday. And I don't want to feel like I am pressured into trying to finish by today, if she is going to take most of the time. And much of it is identifying photographs that have already been identified you've already heard what they are.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm moving as quickly as I can. A lot of these photographs, the Kozarac photos have not been identified by other witnesses. They were introduced for the first time today.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, can you please look at the paragraph when it talks about the number of policemen in the Prijedor, could you please read that paragraph? 107 policemen?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We still need, I think, a text in English put on the ELMO so that we can follow.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Usher?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's too small. We need that --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, can you please read the sentence talking about the number of policemen from the Prijedor municipality?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Prior to the breakout of war, there were 107 active policemen, out of which there were 26 from the Kozarac area. A number of these policemen were killed in combat operations and the others are in the collection centre."

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could you also read out the final paragraph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27
utterances.text: "The war structure anticipates 1342 members in general police stations and 52 members in the road safety station. Out of that number, 1214 should be reserve and 180 active police officers. The previous war structure anticipated 630 policemen. The new war structure, which is functioning now, was prepared during secret preparations for the takeover. It is believed that this war structure can ensure the successful performance of police duties and tasks."

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you. I have finished with that document. You also named other persons that you knew who were either killed or that disappeared in 1992, and that was at page 4316 of the transcript and following.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wish to go into private session now to deal with the final two -- final three aspects of this witness's testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Let's -- Madam Chuqing, let's go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'll do my best, Your Honour, to make sure that we don't make a mistake in that regard. And I think we need to be in private session right as I begin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I want to go to the actual language of the question, sir, that you were asked by Mr. Lukic about people being released from Omarska. It's come up a couple of times today. When people were brought into Omarska they were fairly routinely questioned and interrogated, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27
utterances.text: I've already said that during the first five or six days, there were cases where people were released after interrogation.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Well, let me -- let me remind you of the actual question you were asked and the answer you gave in the Stakic case. When you testified in that case, you took an oath just like you did here today, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You gave truthful testimony in Stakic, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You weren't trying to mislead the judges in Stakic or tell them anything that wasn't true, were you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27
utterances.text: Just like today, because there is no need for me to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The question you were asked was this: Page 4390. "Are you familiar with the fact that during the first ten days of the month of June, quite a few people, approximately 70 per day, were released from the camp having previously been interrogated?" Answer: "Yes, I am." Now that was the question and that was the answer you gave, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And if it's approximate 70 people per day over a ten day period, we are talking 700 people, aren't we?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: After the time that you were in Omarska, I think on 6 August, you said you were sent by bus to Manjaca then.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: About -- would you agree with me it's about 60 kilometres from Omarska to Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27
utterances.text: Approximately, but I don't know the exact figure.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can you tell us how it was that it took all night for the buses to get from Omarska to Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27
utterances.text: I really don't know about that. You should put that question to people who escorted us there and drove us there, because on a bus where I was, there were some 80 to 100 people, and I have no idea how we got there. I just know that we got there. It's difficult to estimate how much time it took us to get there but it definitely was in the morning hours of the following day.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Well, do you have a sense that the buses were going like 6 or 7 kilometres an hour or were they going faster than that or...

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27
utterances.text: I simply didn't think at the time, either about the bus or about its speed. I simply thought about where we were being taken. I was lying on the floor with four or five people on top of me. So I really can't tell you what speed they drove at. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You were -- you were in Manjaca between the 6th of August and the 24th of September, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And so this person who you claim to have been Brdjanin that came to visit there would had to have come during that period of time, between 6 August and 24 September, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And can you be any more precise about when it was that this person who you claim to have been Brdjanin actually came there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27
utterances.text: I've already said that I don't know the exact date of their arrival. Because I didn't conduct any preparations for any trial. It's just that I am now saying about what I still remember after ten years to be truth. I can't tell you the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: But it may have been an error in the translation because I didn't ask you for the exact date. What I asked you was whether you could come closer than sometime between 6 August and 24 September. Was it closer to 6th August or closer to 24 September? Was it closer to the time when you first got there or the time you left?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27
utterances.text: It was closer to the time when we left, because Mr. Brdjanin told us that they were trying to do their utmost to send us to third countries.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Were you actually in Manjaca until the 18th of December?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27
utterances.text: I really don't know. I have two dates. On the 18th was the event with the first group, because we left Manjaca in three groups. So it's either the 18th or the 24th. The best way would be to receive information from the ICRC as to when I left. It was either the 18th or the 24th. But the camp was disbanded somewhere around that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Well, I'm confused between two bits of testimony today. I asked you if were you there between 6 and 24 September and you said you were but on page 31, line 11 of your earlier testimony today, you said you were there until the 18th of December. Did you leave in September or December?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27
utterances.text: It's probably a mistake, but I left in December. There is no doubt about that. I have documents issued by the ICRC.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I think it's probably more my mistake than yours, sir.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So the time when you claim Mr. Brdjanin there would have been closer to the 24th of December than August when you first went there. I think that's where we had gotten to, hadn't we?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you want to break now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have been sitting for another hour and a half. How long more do you anticipate you require, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's difficult to tell. I'll try to finish by 6.30. I might be able to. I can't say that I will. I have quite a bit left to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. We will break for 15 minutes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman. One moment until he puts his headphones on. Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, we were talking about Manjaca and the visit to Manjaca of a person who you claim to have been Mr. Brdjanin. It's the case, isn't it, that the person who came there and went to each of the stables and spoke to all of the detainees claimed to be the President of the Autonomous Region of Krajina, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27
utterances.text: I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you remember that person claiming to have any kind of a position?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you know what position it was that Mr. Brdjanin held in November and December of 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If -- if other people say that the person who came in and addressed the detainees about being released and sent to third countries was Vojo Kupresanin, would you agree that you could be mistaken about who it was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27
utterances.text: I wouldn't agree with that because I saw Mr. Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: In your testimony in the Stakic case, -- let me go -- we'll come back to that. In your testimony in the Stakic case, you were talking about that period of time right after the takeover in Prijedor and at page 4264, you talked about checkpoints that were set up. You told the Court in Stakic that there were checkpoints in Kozarac, near the bridge in Kalata, near the church in Kozarac, at the cross roads on the Prijedor-Banja Luka road, at the entrance to Kozarac, and all the places leading into Kozarac. And you said that those checkpoints were manned by persons of mixed ethnicity, both Muslims and Serbs were manning those checkpoints. That's correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could you give us the names of any of the Serbs that were part of those checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27
utterances.text: You could see Ilija Sarajlic, Ljuban Lukic, Brane Bolta who worked at Kozarac at that time. These two were reserve police officers. Goran Babic, an active military person, who was also at Kozarac as a police officer. Then from Balte, there was Drago -- I can't remember his last name, but in any case, at that point, they were part of the police reserve forces, both Serbs and Muslims in Kozarac were part of those preserve forces when the checkpoints were set up.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes. And these people you've named, the Serbs you named, were along with Muslims manning those checkpoints, is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Now, we talked a few moments ago about the Kozarac police stopping and disarming what you called the Chetnik reservists. You agreed when Mr. Lukic asked you at page 4369 of the Stakic transcript, that the police really have no authority to stop and disarm military, that that's a function of the military police? Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So that really was being done as a provocation, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27
utterances.text: I don't know what kind of a provocation that would be. If no one was -- if it wasn't a question of the Yugoslav army at that time, I didn't understand who the provocation would be directed at. The question is not clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Well, it worked quite well, as a provocation, because each time it was done, it got the authorities in Prijedor all upset and they make threats against Kozarac, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think on page 4369 the witness is talking -- Mr. Lukic said that soldiers could only be taken in and arrested by the military police. I don't know that they were talking about confiscating weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Precise, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The question you were asked, sir, was this: "Are you aware of the fact that soldiers can only be taken in and arrested by the military police?" Your answer was, "Yes, I'm aware of that but this is applicable in a country where laws are obeyed and observed." That was actually your testimony and the question you were asked, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And when you say that it's applicable in a country where laws are obeyed and observed, you apparently were taking the position that at that time in early 1992, laws were not being observed and that it was a time of lawlessness and anarchy in that part of the world, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I think maybe this needs to be in private session, Your Honour, just as a bonus to the question, let's do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go in private session, Madam Registrar. Please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: After you left Bosnia-Herzegovina and having been released from Manjaca, you resided in a third country as a refugee, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And there came a time when that country was getting ready to expel you from the country, didn't there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You know a person by the name of Judge Adil Draganovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you -- you know, don't you that Judge Adil Draganovic wrote a letter on your behalf regarding your situation about expulsion from that third country, don't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27
utterances.text: Yes. [redacted]. I said that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And you know that Judge Draganovic asked that a statement that you had made, which he referred to as a statement given by a detainee from the Keraterm concentration camp, you know that -- that he asked that that statement be forwarded to The Hague Tribunal and that it be done so that the above witness, that being you, who faces expulsion, can remain in this third country and enjoy some amount of protection? That's what was asked by Judge Draganovic in this communication to be sent to The Hague Tribunal, to the OTP, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27
utterances.text: Yes. That is all true, but if you permit me, I would ask you to ask Mr. Stakic, Brdjanin and those others who forced me in 1992 to beg somebody in one of those third countries to keep me because, in Bosnia, in the country where I lived normally, it was not possible at that time for me to return because of my fear due to everything.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
